strengths: Principled theoretical formulation: Viewing residual connections through the lens of continuous-time probability flow ODEs provides a mathematically grounded justification for block-wise training via denoising score matching, avoiding the heuristic or contrastive local loss functions common in prior literature.

Well-motivated partitioning strategy: The proposed equi-probability partitioning distributes noise intervals according to cumulative probability mass under the log-normal distribution, which is systematically ablated and shown to outperform uniform spacing across various layer distributions.

Broad empirical exploration across diverse architectures: The authors evaluate the framework across vision transformers (ViT), image diffusion (DiT), discrete masked language models (MD4), autoregressive transformers, and recurrent-depth architectures (Huginn), showing versatility across modalities and paradigms.

Substantial training memory reduction: Restricting backpropagation to a single block at a time yields a practical $B\times$ reduction in activation memory during training without suffering catastrophic performance degradation.
weaknesses: Inference paradigm shifts and overhead for feedforward/classification tasks: For tasks like image classification (ViT), standard single-pass forward propagation is replaced with an iterative denoising process over label embeddings. This adds multi-step sampling complexity and latency at test time compared to conventional neural networks.

Non-standard evaluation metrics for autoregressive text generation: Because the diffusion formulation does not directly yield token likelihoods/ELBO, the AR model comparison in Table 4 relies solely on MAUVE and external teacher perplexity. While understandable, this makes it harder to assess whether the underlying language model maintains true next-token probability calibration.

Sub-optimal baseline scales and absolute performance: The ViT experiments are conducted on CIFAR-100 with a small custom architecture achieving ~45.5% accuracy, which is substantially below modern vision transformer benchmarks. Demonstrating scalability on standard-sized models on full ImageNet classification would make the empirical validation much stronger.

Missing detailed wall-clock and convergence speed analysis: While peak activation memory is reduced by $B\times$, training blocks independently by uniformly sampling noise levels may affect overall sample efficiency. The paper lacks a comprehensive wall-clock time comparison detailing total GPU hours and iterations needed to match end-to-end convergence.

strengths: Principled and creative theoretical perspective: Connecting residual network architectures to Euler discretizations of continuous-time reverse diffusion ODEs provides a clean, well-grounded formulation for block-independent training via denoising score matching.

Equi-probability noise partitioning: Partitioning the noise schedule according to equal cumulative probability mass under the training noise distribution (log-normal EDM) is mathematically sound and demonstrably superior to naive uniform noise partitioning.

Diverse experimental breadth: The authors validate the framework across a wide spectrum of tasks and architectures, including image generation (DiT), masked diffusion language modeling (MD4), autoregressive LLMs, recurrent-depth models (Huginn), and image classification (ViT).

Concrete computational benefits for diffusion and recurrent models: For DiT and recurrent-depth models, the method naturally delivers notable training memory reduction (proportional to block count B) and avoids unrolling recurrence steps without sacrificing generation quality.
weaknesses: Substantial alteration of non-diffusion tasks and inference dynamics: For standard feedforward classification (ViT) and autoregressive generation, the method does not merely replace backpropagation; it fundamentally redefines the inference process into multi-step iterative denoising (e.g., iterative label embedding denoising or continuous text embedding diffusion), which introduces sampling latency and architectural modifications (e.g., AdaLN conditioning, sequence concatenation).

Weak vision classification performance: The CIFAR-100 ViT baseline attains only ~45.5% accuracy (likely due to training a tiny 128-dim ViT from scratch without pretraining), which is significantly below standard benchmarks. Furthermore, the only block-wise baseline compared is the Forward-Forward algorithm, omitting well-established greedy/local backprop methods (e.g., Belilovsky et al., Nøkland & Eidnes).

Evaluation discrepancies on language modeling: Because autoregressive models are reformulated as continuous embedding diffusion models, standard perplexity (ELBO-based) cannot be evaluated. Relying on MAUVE and teacher-model generative perplexity complicates direct comparison with canonical autoregressive next-token prediction models.

Sub-optimal performance levels on large benchmarks: On ImageNet-256 DiT-L/2, the reported FIDs (10.63 - 12.09) are relatively high compared to fully converged standard DiT-L/2 models (typically FID < 4.0), suggesting limited training budgets or undertrained checkpoints.

strengths: Interesting conceptual connection: The paper links residual connections in deep networks to the Euler discretization of the probability flow ODE in diffusion models, offering an unconventional angle on modular model execution.

Principled noise partitioning: The equi-probability partitioning strategy based on the cumulative probability mass of the EDM log-normal noise schedule is mathematically well-motivated and shown empirically to outperform uniform noise interval splitting.

Broad exploratory scope: The authors apply the concept across a wide variety of tasks and architectures, including image classification with ViT, image synthesis with DiT, masked language diffusion, autoregressive language modeling, and recurrent-depth networks.
weaknesses: Misaligned framing and conceptual conflation: The paper markets itself as solving the general 'block-wise training' problem for deep neural networks (positioning itself against greedy layer-wise training, Forward-Forward, and local loss methods). However, it does not train standard feedforward networks block-wise. Instead, it reformulates every downstream task into a conditional diffusion process (e.g., iterative label-embedding denoising for ViT classification, continuous embedding diffusion for autoregressive language modeling). At inference time, the model executes a multi-step diffusion sampling trajectory rather than a standard single-pass feedforward execution.

Limited novelty over noise-specialized diffusion ensembles: In diffusion models, the training objective decomposes linearly across noise levels by construction ($\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[L(\sigma)] = \sum_b \int_{\sigma_b}^{\sigma_{b-1}} L(\sigma) p(\sigma) d\sigma$). Training independent sub-networks on partitioned noise ranges is already well established in stage-specific/expert diffusion literature (e.g., eDiff-I, Remix-DiT). Packaging this standard property of diffusion models as a breakthrough in 'block-wise neural network training' is conceptually misleading.

Severely undertrained and weak empirical baselines: The reported quantitative results indicate that most baselines are heavily undertrained or underperforming. For example, ViT on CIFAR-100 reaches only 45.26% accuracy (standard baselines typically exceed 70–80%); DiT on CIFAR-10 reports an FID of 39.83 (well-trained diffusion models on CIFAR-10 achieve FID < 3.0); DiT on ImageNet-256 achieves an FID above 10 (compared to ~2.3 for standard DiT); and the AR baseline on LM1B achieves a MAUVE score of only 0.50. These suboptimal operating points weaken the credibility of the claimed parity with end-to-end backpropagation.

Flawed evaluation protocol for language modeling: Because DiffusionBlocks converts next-token prediction into a continuous embedding diffusion process, it cannot report standard negative log-likelihood or test perplexity. Relying exclusively on MAUVE and 'generative perplexity' (using teacher models to evaluate model-generated continuations) is insufficient, as generative perplexity does not penalize mode collapse or hallucination.

Unaccounted computational and architectural overhead: In tasks like classification and language modeling, each block must separately condition on and attend to the conditioning context $x$ while denoising $z_\sigma$. This adds AdaLN conditioning and parameter overhead to each block and scales context-processing compute linearly with the number of blocks/denoising steps at inference time, which is not factored into the efficiency claims.

strengths: The intuition of partitioning the diffusion noise schedule according to cumulative probability mass under the EDM log-normal prior is logical and cleanly formulated.
The paper is generally well-structured and provides systematic ablations on the noise partitioning strategy, overlap coefficient, and block count.
The motivation to reduce memory and compute overheads during training of generative models is timely and practically important.
weaknesses: Conceptual disconnect and misleading framing: The paper presents the method as a novel blockwise/layerwise training paradigm that overcomes backpropagation bottlenecks in deep architectures (positioning against Forward-Forward, greedy layerwise pretraining, and NoProp). However, the actual method simply partitions the diffusion time/noise interval into B segments and trains B independent, shallower denoisers (each with its own input embedding and output projection). The inference procedure (Algorithm 2) is a standard ODE solver operating in data space across multiple steps, rather than a single forward pass through a deep feature hierarchy. Framing a time-partitioned ensemble of denoisers as layerwise training of deep neural networks is conceptually misleading.

Trivial memory reduction: The claimed B-fold memory saving during training is trivial because each block is simply a standalone network containing only L/B layers. Because every block requires its own input/output heads, total parameter count actually increases, and the memory savings are merely the obvious outcome of training smaller models independently.

Poor generation quality and weak experimental numbers: The reported generation results are substantially below standard benchmarks in the diffusion literature. On CIFAR-10, an FID of ~41.4 is very poor (standard DDPM/EDM architectures routinely achieve FIDs below 3.0), and the generated samples in Figure 3 show severe visual degradation and lack of coherent structure. On ImageNet-256, an FID around 15.5 is likewise far below standard DiT baselines.

Lack of empirical hardware measurements: Despite memory reduction being the core selling point, the paper includes no empirical wall-clock time, GPU peak memory (VRAM) profiling, or throughput measurements to substantiate the theoretical claims.

Missing relevant baselines and literature: The paper overlooks established literature on time-dependent multi-expert diffusion models (e.g., eDiff-I, segmented/piecewise diffusion models), which divide the diffusion process into distinct time/noise regimes across specialized subnetworks.

strengths: The core idea of partitioning the diffusion noise schedule into disjoint sub-intervals and assigning independent sub-networks to each interval is intuitive.

The equi-probability noise partitioning scheme based on the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the EDM noise schedule provides a reasonable heuristic for assigning interval boundaries compared to naive uniform spacing in log-noise space.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw and conflation of depth vs. diffusion time: The paper purports to present a blockwise/layerwise alternative to backpropagation for deep neural networks (analogous to greedy layerwise learning, synthetic gradients, or the Forward-Forward algorithm). However, the method does not train a deep network blockwise. Instead, it trains an ensemble of $B$ independent, shallow denoisers (each having $L/B$ layers) specialized to different noise intervals $[\sigma_i, \sigma_{i+1}]$ across diffusion time. The claim in Section 2.3 that internal residual connections in deep networks implement the Euler discretization of reverse diffusion is a conceptual category error: residual connections inside a layer transform representations within a single forward pass, whereas reverse diffusion ODE steps occur in data space across diffusion time steps.

Severely undertrained models and uncompetitive empirical results: The reported FID on CIFAR-10 is 41.39 (and 41.87 for the baseline), which is exceptionally poor for modern diffusion models (standard DiT and DDPM/EDM models on CIFAR-10 routinely reach FIDs below 3.0). The generated samples in Figure 3 confirm that the model produces blurry, low-quality blobs. Evaluating models in such an undertrained regime undermines the validity of any conclusions regarding relative performance.

Unfair inference speedup comparison: The paper claims a 3x to 4x speedup during inference over the baseline. However, this speedup arises trivially because the proposed approach evaluates a shallow $(L/B)$-layer network at each ODE step, whereas the baseline evaluates the full $L$-layer network. The paper fails to compare against an end-to-end baseline with equivalent inference compute (i.e., a model trained with only $L/B$ layers across the entire noise range).

Missing relevant literature on time-specialized / ensemble diffusion models: Decomposing the reverse diffusion process into noise-dependent expert networks is an existing technique in diffusion modeling (e.g., eDiff-I / ensemble of expert denoisers), which is neither cited nor compared against.

Citation and technical inaccuracies: In Section D.2, the authors attribute the 'Vectorized Training approach from Block Diffusion' to '(Siddiqui et al., 2024)', but Siddiqui et al. is an SSL paper ('Blockwise self-supervised learning at scale'), whereas Block Diffusion is by Arriola et al. Furthermore, discrete diffusion language modeling using SEDD is inappropriately merged with continuous score-based formulas and normalized cross-entropy without sufficient mathematical formulation.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting motivation: reducing the activation memory footprint associated with end-to-end backpropagation in deep neural networks.
The idea of partitioning the noise schedule based on equal cumulative probability mass (equi-probability partitioning) is intuitively explained and well-motivated for non-uniform noise schedules.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw regarding residual connections and diffusion time: The paper conflates the depth of a neural network with the time variable of a diffusion process. In Section 2.3, the authors argue that skip connections in ResNets and Transformers naturally implement the Euler discretization of the reverse diffusion PF-ODE, and claim that architectures without skip connections would require implicit ODE solvers. This is mathematically incorrect. The PF-ODE is integrated over continuous diffusion time/noise levels across external sampling steps in data space. The internal residual layers of the denoiser network operate at a fixed diffusion timestep and have no mathematical equivalence to Euler steps along the diffusion trajectory.

Misleading formulation and framing: The paper presents itself as a general blockwise training framework to replace end-to-end backpropagation (comparing itself to greedy layerwise learning, synthetic gradients, and the forward-forward algorithm). In reality, the proposed method simply divides the diffusion noise interval into B sub-intervals and trains B independent, smaller models (e.g., four separate 3-layer DiT networks instead of one 12-layer DiT), each serving as a specialized denoiser for that sub-range. The layers are never sequentially composed in a single forward pass; during inference, each diffusion step invokes only the corresponding small denoiser. Framing this as a general alternative to backpropagation for deep neural networks is fundamentally misleading.

Severely degraded empirical results: The reported generation quality is substantially below accepted standards. On CIFAR-10, the method achieves an FID of 41.39 (and the baseline achieves 41.87), whereas standard diffusion models on CIFAR-10 routinely achieve FID scores below 3.0. The visual samples in Figure 3 clearly exhibit severe artifacts and lack of fidelity. Similarly, the language generation evaluation is limited to MAUVE scores, omitting standard perplexity metrics, and the qualitative text sample in Table 6 is incoherent.

Missing literature on expert and piecewise denoisers: The concept of partitioning the diffusion time/noise schedule across multiple independent networks or experts is well-established in the literature (e.g., eDiff-I by Balaji et al., 2022; Time-dependent Expert Denoisers), yet this line of work is neither cited nor compared against.

Impracticality for autoregressive tasks: While the paper claims to provide memory-efficient training for language modeling, converting autoregressive language modeling into a diffusion process requires tens of diffusion steps per token during inference, creating massive computational inference overhead that counteracts practical utility.
